January 30
Epiphany 4C — The Fourth Sunday of Epiphany 
Colors: green
Lk 4:21-32
1 Cor 14:12-25
Jer 1:4-10
Psalm 71:12-21
To the Saints at Vanadium Woods,
January 30, 2022
Grace and peace from our Lord Jesus Christ, the son of our Father in Heaven, who teaches us his eternal ways.


Last week, I promised I would reveal the exciting conclusion to last week’s Gospel reading this week (Luke 4:21-32). Would you be surprised to learn that, in the end, the hometown crowd did not like what Jesus had to say? As Luke tells the story, at first, they thought well of Jesus, but as he continues to teach about himself as the Messiah in his own synagogue, the congregants become angry with him; they drive him out of the synagogue and attempt to kill him. Jesus does not allow this to happen.


As I usually do, I started to ask myself why St. Luke is telling us this story. The story, taken in isolation, sounds more like a proverb — "no prophet is honored in his hometown" — than it sounds like the teaching of or about Jesus. What can we learn then? The first thing we learn is that this story is not to be taken in isolation!


I just love an obvious answer!


We have to ask where the story begins and where it ends. We cannot depend on chapter and verse as delimiters — none of the Scripture writers used them. We use them because they are convenient, but the writers of Scripture were just writing. I find it interesting that Jesus never referred to chapter and verse in citing passages from the Old Testament. 


But I digress.


I think we should consider the beginning of this story to be when Jesus returns from the wilderness, having been tempted by the devil. As we are told, the devil comes to Jesus with three different temptations, and Jesus does not heed any of them.


Following this, Jesus makes his way to Nazareth, where he announces to his hometown congregation that he is the Messiah. In turn, the hometown congregation does not heed Jesus' words. I hope you can see the parallel between Jesus not listening to the devil and the congregation not listening to Jesus.


This scene in the Synagogue, in literary terms, foreshadows all of Jesus' ministry. At first he was well thought of, then folks started to wonder how he could know so much. Eventually, he made the wrong people angry and they attempted to kill him. But he makes his way through the angry religious people and leaves Nazareth.


What happens after he leaves Nazareth sounds typical of Jesus; he teaches and heals a bunch of people, but St. Luke focuses on two specific instances. The first, in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus commands an unclean spirit to come out of a man and it does. Following his time in the Synagogue, Jesus goes to Simon's (AKA Peter) house.


Now Simon’s mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf.


And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. (Luke 4:38b-39)


Besides these 2 specific instances, St. Luke adds


And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. (Luke 4:41)


If we were to summarize this 4th chapter it would go like this: Jesus doesn't listen to the devil, Jesus' hometown synagogue doesn't listen to Jesus, people in other towns listen to Jesus, and finally the demons listen to Jesus and do what they are told.


To me, this sounds like the storyteller's version of what St. John says of Jesus at the beginning of his Gospel


He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,  who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. (John 1:10-13)


Of the synagogue in Nazareth: I guess familiarity breeds contempt. Contempt bred from familiarity is a very real danger. People all around us have wisdom we could all benefit from. Not that everyone is wise all the time. Using myself as an example - which is always safer - I have been known to say stupid stuff from time to time, far more often than I would like. Careful discernment is always in order when listening to the wisdom of others, but ignoring the wisdom of others because we are familiar with some of their non-wisdom is never in order.


All that being said, the Church we are all a part of is always in danger of treating the words of Jesus with familiar contempt, not out of malice, but more out of a superficial understanding of Jesus. 


In seminary, we would hear lots of apocrypha stories about preachers and pastors - who knew if they were true, but they all had a point. One went like this: The congregation had just hired a new pastor, and everyone was excited to hear his first sermon, and everyone was amazed when they heard it. The second week, he preached the exact same sermon, which was a little weird, but, Ok. On the third Sunday it was the same sermon again, and the same on the fourth Sunday. At this point, the Church board had had enough, and they called a special meeting with the new pastor, whereupon they asked him how come he kept preaching the same sermon. He replied, "When you start living the first sermon, I'll move on to the second."


As to long term employment in the Church, I do not recommend this strategy. Still, we can take that preacher's point: hearing is not living. Jesus had the same sort of criticism about the Scribes and the Pharisees. They knew the Bible of their age frontwards, backward, and inside out, but they did not know how to live it.


Those of us who grew up in the Church are susceptible to the same problems. What's worse is those of us in the preaching business are more likely to succumb to the problems of familial contempt because we have our heads buried in this stuff constantly. I am sure you have all heard the stories, or know the stories personally, of clergy who could benefit the Church by taking up a career in selling Amway.


Be that as it may, while we might have the inclination to treat the teaching of Scripture as the same old, same old, by the grace of God we also have the freedom to listen and apply the revelation of God to new and perhaps interestingly faithful ways.


To sum up, just because we have heard it all before doesn't make what we’ve heard unimportant and not worth paying attention to. The freedom of our lives in Christ gives us the ability to see the world as Our Father sees it and be a part of His Kingdom, even now, but also forever more.


The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of His Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always.
